titulo.texto: Mask of the Dance of the Viejitos (Little Old Men)

frase_gancho.texto: A smiling old man who dances with the energy of a youth.

puente_narrativo.texto: We move from the festival to work with fire. Look for large vessels of reddish copper, their surfaces covered in small round marks, as if they were dotted.

guion_corto.texto: This wooden mask, painted pink, represents a smiling old man. It has flushed cheeks, deep wrinkles, few teeth and white hair made of ixtle fiber. It comes from the region of Lake Pátzcuaro, and it is part of the Dance of the Viejitos (Little Old Men), one of the best-known dances in Mexico. It is danced by young men dressed as old men and leaning on canes. At first they walk hunched over and clumsy, as if every step were a struggle, and then suddenly they surprise the audience with a fast, powerful stomping of their feet. The dance plays with laughter, respect for elders and the energy that, even with the years, is still alive.

guion_largo.texto:
A mask can be frightening, like the one of the Cora Jew, or it can make you laugh. This one makes you laugh. It represents an old man with ruddy cheeks, a mouth almost without teeth, deep wrinkles and white hair made of ixtle fiber. He looks as if he had just told a joke. And with it begins one of the most famous dances in Mexico.

The Viejitos are danced mainly in the region of Lake Pátzcuaro, in towns such as the island of Jarácuaro. The dancers, who are young, dress up as old men: mask, straw hat with colorful ribbons that fall over the shoulders, and cane. The cane helps them pretend to be tired, even though later it is used to mark the rhythm on the ground. They begin hunched over, with timid steps, as if everything hurt. And suddenly, without warning, they straighten up and stomp with an energy that is not an old man’s. The audience bursts into laughter and applause. Surprise is the heart of the dance.

Why laugh at old age? There are several readings. One says it is a tribute: elders are the wisest, and they are treated with humor because they are loved. Another says it expresses the idea that life does not end with the years. There are even those who link the dance to the ancient veneration of an old god of fire, like the [Huehuetéotl](mna_s04_huehueteotl) you saw in Teotihuacán, although that connection is debated. What is certain is that people love the dance.

Look closely at the mask. It is carved from light wood, usually avocado, and painted in pinkish tones. The ixtle hair is the same maguey fiber used to weave the bundles of Candelaria and to make sacks and ropes. The materials of the festival are those of everyday life.

Music accompanies the dance. It is string music, with guitars and violins, and rhythms that invite you to dance. Many Purépecha towns also have the pirekua, a traditional song in their language that UNESCO recognized in the year two thousand ten as intangible cultural heritage of humanity. That music and that dance are part of what makes this region so recognizable.

The region of Lake Pátzcuaro is also famous for another celebration: the Night of the Dead, when families keep vigil in the cemeteries, with candles and flowers, and the island of Janitzio fills with light. In the Huastecs and Totonacs Hall you will see an [altar of the dead](mna_s18_altar_xantolo), and you will understand how that offering is prepared.

The Dance of the Viejitos became famous throughout the country during the twentieth century, and today it is danced on stages, in competitions and at festivals. But above all, it remains something that belongs to its community. Whoever puts on the mask becomes someone else for a while. And the little old man who dances is really a young man who wants his town to laugh. Perhaps the best part of the dance is that mixture: an affectionate joke about old age and a reminder that strength never completely goes away.

texto: Notice the rosy cheeks, the smile and the wrinkles
Touch with your eyes the white hair made of ixtle fiber
Look for the eye openings: how does the dancer see?

texto.Region: Shores and islands of Lake Pátzcuaro (Jarácuaro, Michoacán)
texto.Technique/Material: Carved avocado/ash wood, enamel paint, ixtle, and wax
texto.Function: Ritual masking paraphernalia for the dance of the patron saint festival

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Dance of the Viejitos is performed by real old men.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is danced by young men dressed as old men. The charm lies in the surprise: they begin hunched over and suddenly stomp with force.
